meta.title: Rocket Lab Corporation — Peter Beck's small-launch and space-systems franchise approaching Neutron
meta.subtitle: From the 2006 Auckland startup through the 2021 SPAC listing to a $1B+ revenue trajectory and the 2026 Neutron medium-lift debut
meta.abstract: Rocket Lab Corporation (RKLB, NASDAQ) is the Long Beach, California-headquartered (with major operations in New Zealand) launch and space systems company founded in 2006 by Peter Beck. The company is the second-most-active US-listed commercial launch operator after SpaceX through 2024-2026, with the Electron small launch vehicle having completed 60-plus orbital missions since its 2018 first successful flight, plus a substantial and growing space systems business that provides spacecraft buses, components, and subsystems to commercial, civil, and US national security customers. Peter Beck continues as Chief Executive Officer and Chairman of the Board through the public-company period (Rocket Lab went public via SPAC business combination with Vector Acquisition Corporation in August 2021); CFO Adam Spice has been in role since 2018 providing multi-year continuity. The Neutron medium-lift vehicle development is the central forward strategic programme — Neutron targets approximately 13,000 kilograms to low Earth orbit (compared to Electron's approximately 300 kilograms) and is intended to enter commercial service in 2026 to compete in the medium-lift commercial and national security launch markets where SpaceX's Falcon 9 is the dominant US incumbent. Fiscal year 2025 (calendar year 2025) revenue exceeded $400 million across the launch services and space systems segments; the FY2025 operating loss was substantial reflecting the Neutron development capex and broader R&D investment. The company has been one of the most consistent operational executors in the US small launch industry plus one of the more strategically-positioned space systems suppliers; the Neutron commercial debut in 2026 is the central forward catalyst that will materially affect the equity trajectory. The board includes directors with deep aerospace, defence, and venture capital backgrounds; the executive team is built around Peter Beck's founder leadership plus the post-SPAC public-company financial and operational infrastructure.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Rocket Lab Corporation (RKLB, Nasdaq) had, by the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, become much more than the listed small-launch specialist that public investors first met in the August 2021 SPAC merger. The company still rested on Electron, the dedicated small launcher Peter Beck had built around schedule control and orbit specificity, but the business mix had shifted decisively toward spacecraft, components, and national-security work. Electron had reached 88 launches by 22 May 2026, and Rocket Lab described it that day as the world's most frequently launched orbital small rocket after completing its ninth dedicated Synspective mission, "Viva La StriX," from Launch Complex 1 in New Zealand [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/mission-success-rocket-lab-completes-9th-electron-launch) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/electron/).

## Corporate Anatomy

Rocket Lab had reported through two operating segments: Launch Services and Space Systems. Launch Services encompassed Electron, HASTE, and Neutron. Electron's official published specification at the snapshot date was a payload of 300 kilograms to low Earth orbit on a vehicle standing 18 metres tall with a wet mass of 13,000 kilograms, flying from Launch Complex 1 in Mahia and Launch Complex 2 at Wallops Island, Virginia [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/electron/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-successfully-launches-first-electron-mission-from-u-s-soil/). Neutron, still in development, was Rocket Lab's 13,000-kilogram reusable medium-launch bet, aimed squarely at constellation deployment, national security launch, and exploration missions [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/neutron/).

Space Systems had become the larger commercial engine. The portfolio had been assembled in steps that were often described loosely in earlier market commentary but were more precise in Rocket Lab's own record: Sinclair Interplanetary closed in April 2020; Advanced Solutions, Inc. closed in October 2021; Planetary Systems Corporation closed in December 2021; SolAero Holdings closed in January 2022; and Geost, the electro-optical and infrared payload maker, closed in August 2025 [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-satellite-hardware-manufacturer-sinclair-interplanetary/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-acquires-space-software-company-advanced-solutions-inc/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-hardware-company-planetary-systems-corporation/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-solar-power-products-company-solaero-holdings-inc/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-geost-expanding-its-national). The SPAC merger with Vector Acquisition Corporation closed on 25 August 2021 and delivered roughly $777 million of gross proceeds, not the smaller figure often repeated in summary writeups [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-completes-merger-vector-acquisition-corporation).

## The Numbers

The revenue arc still looked exceptional by aerospace standards, but the freshest numbers inside the frozen window came from both the 2025 Form 10-K and the first-quarter 2026 Form 10-Q. Full-year 2025 revenue was $601.8 million, up 38% from $436.2 million in 2024 and more than double the $244.6 million posted in 2023. Space Systems contributed $402.8 million of 2025 revenue and Launch Services $199.0 million, confirming that Rocket Lab's economic centre of gravity had moved away from pure launch several years after the market began to value it primarily as a launch name [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm).

| Period | Revenue | Launch Services | Space Systems |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $244.6M | $71.9M | $172.7M |
| FY2024 | $436.2M | $125.4M | $310.8M |
| FY2025 | $601.8M | $199.0M | $402.8M |
| Q1 2026 | $200.3M | $63.7M | $136.7M |

The profit line remained negative, but the balance sheet had strengthened materially. Rocket Lab's 2025 net loss attributable to common stockholders was $198.2 million and operating loss was $228.8 million. In the March 2026 quarter, revenue reached a record $200.3 million while operating loss narrowed to $56.0 million and net loss to $45.0 million. Backlog rose from $1.85 billion at year-end 2025 to $2.22 billion at 31 March 2026, with $1.30 billion in Space Systems and $921.4 million in Launch Services. Cash and cash equivalents stood at $1.205 billion at quarter-end, with another $271.3 million of marketable securities on the balance sheet [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 Results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000027/rklb-05072026ex991.htm).

Those liquidity figures reflected unusually aggressive capital raising. During 2025 the company sold 15.66 million shares for approximately $749.4 million of gross proceeds under its prior at-the-market programme, and in April 2026 it said it had completed a second ATM programme that sold 6.73 million shares for roughly $474 million of gross proceeds while also entering collared forward transactions over another 7.45 million shares for expected gross proceeds of roughly $474 million to $642 million [Rocket Lab Prospectus Supplement](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/static-files/d367305d-382d-42c3-b269-969947c5f64f) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-completes-market-offering). By 31 March 2026, only $37.6 million principal amount of the 4.25% convertible notes remained outstanding after conversions earlier in the quarter [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm).

## Customer Base

By the snapshot date the company had become deeply embedded in U.S. national-security procurement. Rocket Lab National Security won a $515 million Space Development Agency award in January 2024 to build and operate 18 Tranche 2 Transport Layer-Beta satellites, and in December 2025 Rocket Lab won an $816 million SDA award to build 18 Tracking Layer Tranche 3 satellites - the largest single contract disclosed in the company's history through the frozen window [SDA](https://www.sda.mil/space-development-agency-makes-third-award-to-build-18-additional-beta-variant-satellites-for-tranche-2-transport-layer/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-awarded-816m-prime-contract-build-missile-defense). Neutron was on-ramped to the U.S. Space Force's $5.6 billion NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1 programme in March 2025, expanding the addressable launch market before the rocket had flown [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-labs-neutron-rocket-ramped-us-space-forces-56b-national) [Space Systems Command](https://www.ssc.spaceforce.mil/Newsroom/Article/4137680/space-systems-command-on-ramps-two-new-providers-to-national-security-space-lau/).

The launch side still mattered. Rocket Lab won the $32 million VICTUS HAZE tactically responsive space mission in April 2024, a design-build-launch contract that required Electron and a Rocket Lab spacecraft to stand ready for launch within 24 hours of call-up [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-selected-space-systems-command-build-and-launch). In March 2026 it disclosed a four-year, $190 million contract for 20 HASTE launches under MACH-TB 2.0, taking the launch manifest to more than 70 missions in backlog [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-secures-190m-contract-20x-haste-launches-cements).

Commercial launch relationships had become more repeatable than the early small-launch market sceptics had expected. Synspective expanded its deal with Rocket Lab in September 2025, taking its contracted Electron missions to 21. Capella had signed a multi-launch Electron deal in 2023. BlackSky added another four dedicated Electron launches in February 2026. Those were not one-off payloads opportunistically buying rides; they were repeat customers contracting blocks of dedicated missions [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-and-synspective-strike-another-10-launch-deal) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-signs-multi-launch-deal-to-deploy-satellite-constellation-for-capella-space/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-secures-latest-multi-launch-contract-blacksky-4x).

## Neutron: The Medium-Launch Bet

Neutron remained the crucial unresolved variable. Rocket Lab had opened Launch Complex 3 in Virginia in August 2025 and qualified the "Hungry Hippo" captive fairing in December 2025, but a stage-one tank ruptured during hydrostatic qualification testing in January 2026. Rocket Lab said the next tank was already in production and, in the February 2026 full-year results release, shifted first launch to Q4 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-3-critical-milestone-path) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/node/11706/pdf) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-neutron-test-update/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial).

## The Central Question

The snapshot therefore showed a company that had already won the argument that it was more than a boutique launcher, but had not yet answered the harder question of whether it could become a medium-lift launch competitor at scale. Electron had become a real industrial franchise, Space Systems had become the larger revenue engine, and national-security customers had validated Rocket Lab as a prime contractor. The missing proof point was whether Neutron, after the January 2026 tank-test rupture and the slide to a Q4 2026 debut target, could still reach the market inside a commercially useful window. The rest of the dossier turns on that question.

chapters.title: From the 2006 New Zealand founding through Electron, the 2021 SPAC, and Neutron
chapters.body:
## A Workshop in New Zealand, a Rocket in Mahia

Rocket Lab's origin story had become familiar enough to sound polished, but the underlying facts remained unusual for an aerospace company of its scale. Peter Beck began as a precision-engineering apprentice at Fisher & Paykel in 1993, later moved into product and machinery design, and from 2003 worked at a New Zealand government research institute on advanced materials and composites. Rocket Lab's own executive biography said Beck founded the company in 2006 after several years of working on propulsion and structures in parallel with his day job [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about/team/). The company later folded the more cinematic version of that founding into its own brand history, saying Beck had made a "rocket pilgrimage" through the United States in 2006, failed to find a company pursuing the small-satellite launch model he wanted, and decided on the flight home to start Rocket Lab himself [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/introducing-our-new-look/).

The thesis was explicit from the start. Beck argued that the satellite industry would need something other than piggyback access on large launch vehicles. The vehicle built around that view was Electron: a two-stage, carbon-composite rocket powered by nine sea-level Rutherford engines on the first stage and a single vacuum Rutherford on the second. Rocket Lab's own product literature later standardised Electron at 18 metres tall, 13,000 kilograms wet mass, and 300 kilograms to low Earth orbit, with the Rutherford promoted as the first 3D-printed, electric-pump-fed rocket engine to reach orbit [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/electron/).

Launch infrastructure came almost as early as propulsion. Rocket Lab built Launch Complex 1 on the Mahia Peninsula in New Zealand and later described it as the first private orbital launch site in the world. The site gave the company a level of orbital flexibility and scheduling control that was unusual for a launch provider of its size, and the New Zealand regulatory framework had to be built around it before commercial cadence could follow [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/launch-sites/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-successfully-makes-it-to-space-2/).

## Electron's Debut and the Commercial Turn

The first Electron mission, "It's a Test," lifted off on 25 May 2017. It reached space but did not make orbit after a ground-communications problem triggered range safety procedures. Rocket Lab's post-flight review later said the vehicle had otherwise performed well enough to accelerate the return to the pad [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-successfully-makes-it-to-space-2/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-completes-post-flight-analysis/). The second mission, "Still Testing," on 21 January 2018, did what the first one had narrowly missed: it reached orbit and deployed customer payloads, which Rocket Lab itself described as the beginning of a new era in commercial access to space [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-successfully-reaches-orbit-and-deploys-payloads-january-21-2018/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/missions/launches/still-testing/).

The commercial era followed quickly. "It's Business Time," Rocket Lab's third Electron mission, launched on 11 November 2018 carrying spacecraft for Spire Global, Tyvak, Fleet, the Irvine CubeSat STEM Program, and a drag-sail technology demonstrator. Rocket Lab's mission page described it as the company's first fully commercial flight and the fastest transition a private launch provider had made from a test programme to a commercial manifest [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/missions/launches/its-business-time/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-to-launch-first-commercial-mission-this-month/).

Cadence-building came next. The company flew six Electron missions in 2019 and seven in 2020 before expanding again in the public-company years. Those missions diversified the customer base across Earth observation, weather, maritime tracking, research payloads, and U.S. government work. The industrial significance was less about any one launch than about repeated execution: Rocket Lab had moved from a technology demonstration to a flight-proven launch system before most of its later small-launch peers ever left the drawing board [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about-us/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial).

## From Mahia to Virginia

The U.S. launch footprint developed in two phases. Rocket Lab officially opened Launch Complex 2 at Wallops Flight Facility in early 2020 and said at the time that the site had been built to serve U.S. government and commercial customers from domestic soil [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-2-confirms-u-s-air-force-payload-as-first-electron-mission-from-u-s-soil/). The site's operational debut slipped, but the first Electron mission from Virginia - "Virginia is for Launch Lovers" - ultimately flew on 24 January 2023 for HawkEye 360. Rocket Lab called it the company's 33rd Electron mission overall and its first from U.S. soil [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-successfully-launches-first-electron-mission-from-u-s-soil/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/missions/missions-launched/new-mission-page-2/).

That two-site structure became strategically important. Launch Complex 1 preserved the schedule flexibility and orbital geometry that had underpinned Electron's early commercial value proposition. Launch Complex 2 gave Rocket Lab a U.S.-based launch option for customers with domestic-regulatory or national-security preferences. The dual-site setup was one reason Electron remained more commercially relevant than its modest payload mass alone might have suggested [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/launch-sites/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/missions/missions-launched/new-mission-page-2/).

## The SPAC Combination

Rocket Lab entered public markets through its merger with Vector Acquisition Corporation, which closed on 25 August 2021. The company said the transaction delivered approximately $777 million of gross proceeds from the SPAC trust and concurrent PIPE financing, and that the cash would be used to accelerate space-systems growth, fund Neutron, and support further expansion into applications and services [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-completes-merger-vector-acquisition-corporation). The deal did not change the strategic message Beck had been pushing privately. It formalised it. Rocket Lab wanted to be valued not simply as a launcher but as an end-to-end space company.

## The Acquisition Arc

The acquisition history needed more precision than many earlier summaries gave it. The first major step was Sinclair Interplanetary, which closed in April 2020 and brought reaction wheels, star trackers, and other satellite hardware into the portfolio [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-satellite-hardware-manufacturer-sinclair-interplanetary/). After the SPAC close, Rocket Lab accelerated the programme. Advanced Solutions, Inc. closed in October 2021 for spacecraft software, mission simulation, and guidance, navigation and control [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-acquires-space-software-company-advanced-solutions-inc/). Planetary Systems Corporation closed in December 2021, adding separation systems including the Motorized Lightband and satellite dispensers [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-hardware-company-planetary-systems-corporation/). SolAero Holdings closed in January 2022 for $80 million in cash, bringing space-grade solar cells, panels, and precision structures in house [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-solar-power-products-company-solaero-holdings-inc/). Geost followed in August 2025, extending the stack into electro-optical and infrared payloads for missile warning, tracking, and space domain awareness [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-geost-expanding-its-national).

That sequence mattered because it showed what Rocket Lab actually bought. Earlier draft language that referred to a "Plasma" acquisition, or that swapped the timing of PSC and SolAero, did not match Rocket Lab's own announcements. By the snapshot date, the company had assembled a chain that ran from launch to spacecraft bus to components to payloads, with electric propulsion emerging later as an internally engineered product rather than as a disclosed acquisition [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/space-systems/gauss-propulsion/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-unveils-new-electric-propulsion-satellite-thruster).

## Neutron and the Unfinished Timetable

Neutron was announced in March 2021 as Rocket Lab's move into medium launch. The company eventually standardised the vehicle at roughly 13,000 kilograms to low Earth orbit in reusable configuration, with a reusable first stage, a carbon-composite structure, and nine methane-fuelled Archimedes engines on the booster [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/neutron/). The timetable moved several times. Early public targets pointed to 2024, then to the second half of 2025. In January 2026, however, Rocket Lab said a stage-one tank had ruptured during hydrostatic qualification testing; the company maintained that the next tank was already in production, but the February 2026 full-year results release reset the first-launch target to Q4 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-neutron-test-update/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial).

The slippage did not erase the strategic logic. It did, however, crystallise the central tension in Rocket Lab's history through the snapshot date: Electron had already proved that Beck could build and operate a differentiated launch business, while Neutron remained the unproven programme that would determine whether Rocket Lab's addressable market truly widened or merely became more expensive to pursue.

chapters.title: Electron, Neutron, Photon, and the Space Systems components portfolio
chapters.body:
## Two Businesses Sharing One Balance Sheet

Rocket Lab's structure looked cleaner in the filings than it often did in market shorthand. The company reported two segments - Launch Services and Space Systems - but by May 2026 those labels described businesses of very different maturity. Launch Services was the heritage franchise that had given Rocket Lab credibility. Space Systems had become the larger revenue engine, the broader product portfolio, and in several quarters the better demonstration of industrial scale [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm).

## Electron: The Workhorse

Electron remained the cornerstone of Launch Services. Rocket Lab's official specification at the snapshot date was 300 kilograms to LEO on an 18 metre, two-stage carbon-composite vehicle with a Kick Stage option for precise orbital insertion [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/electron/). By 21 December 2025 Rocket Lab said it had completed 21 launches across Electron and HASTE during the year with a 100% mission-success rate, ending 2025 on its 79th launch overall. It then pushed to its 80th Electron launch on 22 January 2026, its 84th on 21 March 2026, and its 88th by 22 May 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-successfully-launches-iqps-ends-2025-21-launches-and) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-delivers-mission-success-first-launch-2026-new) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/mission-success-rocket-lab-launches-latest-satellite-0) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/mission-success-rocket-lab-completes-9th-electron-launch).

The appeal was never raw payload mass. Electron competed by giving customers dedicated launches into customer-specific orbits on customer-specific timetables. That mattered to SAR constellations, responsive-space missions, and government payloads that did not want to accept rideshare sequencing risk. Synspective, iQPS, Capella, BlackSky, HawkEye 360, NASA, and a range of national-security customers had all used Electron or HASTE under that logic [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-and-synspective-strike-another-10-launch-deal) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/iqps-books-three-new-launches-electron-extending-multi-year) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-signs-multi-launch-deal-to-deploy-satellite-constellation-for-capella-space/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-secures-latest-multi-launch-contract-blacksky-4x) [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-contract-to-launch-cubesat-to-moon-from-virginia/).

| Vehicle | Published payload to LEO | Class | Reuse status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electron | 300 kg | Small | Recovery programme in development |
| HASTE | 700 kg suborbital payload | Hypersonic testbed | Derived from Electron |
| Neutron | 13,000 kg reusable | Medium | In development |

Recovery remained developmental rather than industrialised. Rocket Lab had demonstrated helicopter capture in May 2022 and later shifted emphasis toward ocean recovery and hardware reuse work. By 2024 it had returned a previously flown Electron stage to the production line in preparation for reflight, and in earlier work had successfully test-fired a reused Rutherford engine. Those were meaningful steps, but they were not yet equivalent to routine booster reuse at Falcon 9 scale [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-completes-historic-mid-air-helicopter-capture-of-electron-rocket-returning-from-space/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-returns-previously-flown-electron-to-production-line-in-preparation-for-first-reflight/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-successfully-completes-first-test-fire-of-reused-rutherford-engine/).

That launch franchise had also become broader than the standard Electron shorthand implied. HASTE, Rocket Lab's suborbital test vehicle derived from Electron, was marketed by the company at a 700-kilogram payload capacity and as a responsive, cost-effective hypersonic testbed rather than a side experiment [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/haste/). Combined with Mahia's schedule flexibility and Wallops' U.S.-based access, that gave Rocket Lab multiple ways to monetise essentially the same core launch architecture across commercial smallsat, tactically responsive and hypersonic-test demand.

## Neutron: The Strategic Escalation

Neutron was Rocket Lab's attempt to move from a small-launch niche into the much larger medium-lift market. The company presented it as a fully reusable, methane-fuelled vehicle for constellation deployment, national-security launch, civil exploration and eventually human spaceflight, with a published payload of 13,000 kilograms to LEO [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/neutron/). Launch Complex 3 opened in Virginia in August 2025 as a dedicated launch, test and landing site for the vehicle, and the company qualified Neutron's attached "Hungry Hippo" fairing in December 2025 [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-3-critical-milestone-path) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/node/11706/pdf).

But Neutron remained unfinished by the snapshot date. In January 2026 Rocket Lab said a stage-one tank ruptured during hydrostatic qualification testing; in February it moved the first-launch target to Q4 2026. The product still mattered because it widened the addressable market dramatically, but it had not yet contributed revenue [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-neutron-test-update/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial).

## Photon and the Spacecraft Stack

Between Electron and Neutron sat Photon, the spacecraft platform that best captured Rocket Lab's integrated strategy. Photon began life as Electron's Kick Stage and grew into a full satellite bus used for low-Earth-orbit, cislunar and interplanetary missions. CAPSTONE proved the platform in lunar transfer in 2022, while ESCAPADE's twin Rocket Lab-built spacecraft were successfully launched in late 2025 and commissioned at Earth-Sun L2 by February 2026 ahead of their Mars cruise [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-contract-to-launch-cubesat-to-moon-from-virginia/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-completes-spacecraft-commissioning-for-nasas-escapade-mars-mission/).

The component stack around Photon was assembled with more discipline than many earlier drafts implied. Sinclair added reaction wheels and star trackers; ASI added flight software and GNC tools; PSC added separation systems; SolAero added solar cells, panels and precision structures; Geost added EO/IR payloads; and in 2026 Rocket Lab introduced its own Gauss Hall-effect propulsion product rather than disclosing a propulsion-company acquisition [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-satellite-hardware-manufacturer-sinclair-interplanetary/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-acquires-space-software-company-advanced-solutions-inc/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-hardware-company-planetary-systems-corporation/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-solar-power-products-company-solaero-holdings-inc/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-geost-expanding-its-national) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-unveils-new-electric-propulsion-satellite-thruster).

Rocket Lab's own spacecraft pages showed how far that stack had spread by the frozen window. The company marketed a family that spanned Photon, Pioneer, Lightning and Explorer, said it had more than 40 spacecraft in backlog, and said 1,700 spacecraft globally already featured Rocket Lab satellite components [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/spacecraft). That mattered because it reframed Space Systems as a product family with platform reuse and merchant-component scale, not simply as a bundle of acquired parts businesses.

## Why the Mix Changed

The numbers made the structural shift plain. Space Systems had supplied $310.8 million of revenue in 2024 and $402.8 million in 2025, versus $125.4 million and $199.0 million respectively for Launch Services. In Q1 2026 the split was $136.7 million of Space Systems and $63.7 million of Launch Services. Rocket Lab still needed launch to prove schedule reliability and to cross-sell the rest of the stack. But by the frozen snapshot date, the company was no longer economically organised around launch alone [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm).

The quarterly launch figures also suggested that the launch business was getting richer, not just busier. The March 2026 10-Q said Launch Services revenue rose to $63.7 million on six Electron missions, versus $35.6 million on five missions a year earlier, and explicitly attributed the increase not only to cadence but also to higher revenue per launch, over-time HASTE revenue and other launch-related work [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm). That reduced the simplistic view that Electron had become a low-margin commodity launcher whose only purpose was to feed Neutron.

chapters.title: $437M revenue, operating losses, and the Neutron capex trajectory
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Arc That Kept Steepening

Rocket Lab's financial picture had become more complicated than the old "pre-profit launcher" shorthand suggested. The company still lost money, and Neutron still absorbed capital at a rate that made profitability speculative rather than imminent. But the revenue line had continued to steepen through the frozen window. The 2025 Form 10-K reported $601.8 million of revenue, up 38% from $436.2 million in 2024 and up from $244.6 million in 2023. Then the March 2026 quarter came in at a record $200.3 million, versus $122.6 million in the year-earlier period [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm).

| Period | Revenue | YoY growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $62.2M | - |
| FY2022 | $211.0M | 239% |
| FY2023 | $244.6M | 16% |
| FY2024 | $436.2M | 78% |
| FY2025 | $601.8M | 38% |
| Q1 2026 | $200.3M | 63% |

The first point that mattered was that growth had remained broad-based. It was no longer just acquisitions being lapped through the revenue line. The 2025 10-K said Launch Services revenue grew 59% year on year to $199.0 million, while Space Systems grew 30% to $402.8 million. In Q1 2026 Launch Services was up 79% and Space Systems 57%, driven by six Electron launches in the quarter, over-time HASTE revenue, spacecraft manufacturing growth and acquisitions [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm).

## Segment Mix: Space Systems Stayed in Front

The post-SPAC inversion of the business mix continued through the snapshot date.

| Period | Launch Services | Space Systems | Total Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $60.7M | $150.3M | $211.0M |
| FY2023 | $71.9M | $172.7M | $244.6M |
| FY2024 | $125.4M | $310.8M | $436.2M |
| FY2025 | $199.0M | $402.8M | $601.8M |
| Q1 2026 | $63.7M | $136.7M | $200.3M |

That mix meant Rocket Lab's valuation case could no longer be reduced to launch cadence alone. Space Systems contributed roughly 67% of 2025 revenue and 68% of Q1 2026 revenue. The segment also carried the company's biggest disclosed contracts, including the $515 million SDA Tranche 2 award and the $816 million Tracking Layer Tranche 3 award [SDA](https://www.sda.mil/space-development-agency-makes-third-award-to-build-18-additional-beta-variant-satellites-for-tranche-2-transport-layer/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-awarded-816m-prime-contract-build-missile-defense).

## Losses Remained Real, but Gross Profit Improved

Rocket Lab was still pre-profit on a GAAP basis. Operating loss was $177.9 million in 2023, $189.8 million in 2024, and $228.8 million in 2025. Net loss attributable to Rocket Lab common stockholders was $182.6 million in 2023, $190.2 million in 2024, and $198.2 million in 2025 [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm). Yet the gross-profit line had improved faster than the headline loss figures implied. Gross profit rose from $51.4 million in 2023 to $116.1 million in 2024 and $207.2 million in 2025, which meant GAAP gross margin expanded from roughly 21.0% in 2023 to 26.6% in 2024 and 34.4% in 2025 [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm).

The March 2026 quarter continued that pattern. Q1 2026 gross profit was $76.5 million on $200.3 million of revenue, versus $35.2 million on $122.6 million a year earlier. Operating loss improved modestly to $56.0 million from $59.2 million despite a much larger business and higher operating expense [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 Results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000027/rklb-05072026ex991.htm).

| Period | Gross Profit | Gross Margin | R&D as % of Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $51.4M | 21.0% | 48.7% |
| FY2024 | $116.1M | 26.6% | 40.0% |
| FY2025 | $207.2M | 34.4% | 45.0% |
| Q1 2026 | $76.5M | 38.2% | 40.2% |

The segment detail in the March 2026 10-Q was more constructive than the headline operating loss suggested. Launch Services generated $28.2 million of gross profit in the quarter on $63.7 million of revenue, while Space Systems generated $48.3 million on $136.7 million. Inside Space Systems, product revenue was $127.5 million versus only $9.2 million of services, underscoring how much of the growth had moved into manufactured hardware rather than lower-commitment engineering work [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm).

## R&D, SG&A, and What Was Really Being Funded

The expense lines showed why the company remained loss-making. Research and development expense, net, rose from $119.1 million in 2023 to $174.4 million in 2024 and then to $270.7 million in 2025. Selling, general and administrative expense rose from $110.3 million in 2023 to $131.6 million in 2024 and $165.3 million in 2025 [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm).

In Q1 2026, R&D was $80.5 million and SG&A $51.9 million. The 10-Q said the R&D increase was driven primarily by Neutron development progress, added staff, and prototype spend tied to expanding the spacecraft and spacecraft-components product portfolio. The SG&A increase was partly a one-time stock-based compensation effect from RSU cancellations, alongside added staff and transaction costs tied to an active acquisition pipeline [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm).

Rocket Lab discussed Neutron investment in aggregate, but it did not break out a clean Neutron-only line inside quarterly R&D. That mattered because Neutron was clearly the dominant investment programme, but it was not the only one; Rocket Lab was simultaneously scaling spacecraft manufacturing, solar products, payloads, hypersonic systems and new component lines [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-unveils-new-electric-propulsion-satellite-thruster).

## Liquidity: The Story Changed Completely

The balance-sheet story changed more dramatically than the income statement. At 31 December 2024, Rocket Lab had $271.0 million of cash and cash equivalents and $208.6 million of current marketable securities. By 31 December 2025, cash alone had climbed to $828.7 million, with another $270.2 million of marketable securities. By 31 March 2026, cash was $1.205 billion and total marketable securities were $271.3 million, taking total cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities to roughly $1.48 billion [Rocket Lab 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000162828025008724/rklb-20241231.htm) [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm).

That was not organic cash generation. It was capital-market access. First came the February 2024 issuance of $355 million aggregate principal amount of 4.25% convertible senior notes due 2029, accompanied by capped-call transactions and Trinity equipment financing [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-closing-upsized-offering-355-million). Then, during 2025, Rocket Lab sold 15,662,372 shares under its prior ATM programme for approximately $749.4 million of gross proceeds [Rocket Lab Prospectus Supplement](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/static-files/d367305d-382d-42c3-b269-969947c5f64f). Finally, in April 2026, Rocket Lab said it had completed a second ATM programme under which it sold 6,726,862 shares for approximately $474 million of gross proceeds and entered collared forward transactions over another 7,451,200 shares for expected gross proceeds of roughly $474 million to $642 million [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-completes-market-offering).

The dilution was material, but it had also de-risked near-term funding. The Q1 2026 10-Q said net cash provided by financing activities in the quarter was $463.3 million, chiefly from the ATM. It also showed that the outstanding balance on the 2029 convertible notes had been cut to $37.6 million principal by 31 March 2026 after conversions earlier in the quarter [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm).

The share-count effect was therefore impossible to ignore. Weighted-average common shares outstanding rose from 495.9 million in 2024 to 530.7 million in 2025, then to 605.4 million in the March 2026 quarter. The 10-Q also said common shares issued had risen to 621.7 million by 31 March 2026, with 575.8 million outstanding after treasury stock, versus 589.5 million issued and 543.6 million outstanding at year-end 2025 [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm). The balance sheet was far safer, but the per-share hurdle had also moved materially higher.

## Capital Expenditure and Backlog

Capital expenditure was the other window into Neutron's demands. Rocket Lab's purchases of property, equipment and software were $54.7 million in 2023, $67.1 million in 2024, and $156.3 million in 2025. Q1 2026 added another $27.1 million [Rocket Lab 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000162828025008724/rklb-20241231.htm) [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm). That spending matched what the company was physically building: Launch Complex 3 in Virginia, the Neutron integration and manufacturing footprint, the Archimedes test complex at Stennis, the Middle River structures complex, and the Long Beach engine centre [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-3-critical-milestone-path) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-opens-engine-development-center-in-long-beach/).

Backlog suggested that customers were not waiting for Neutron to fly before committing capital. Backlog stood at $1.067 billion at year-end 2024, $1.847 billion at year-end 2025, and $2.220 billion at 31 March 2026. Rocket Lab said in its May 2026 quarterly materials that it had signed 31 new Electron and HASTE launch contracts plus five dedicated Neutron contracts in Q1 alone, and that it had sold more launches in the quarter than in the whole of 2025 [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 Results](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/node/12416/pdf).

That detail mattered because it weakened the bluntest bear argument around Neutron delay. Customers were plainly still willing to commit to Rocket Lab before the medium-lift vehicle had flown. The same quarterly package that disclosed the $2.22 billion backlog also said total launch manifest exceeded 70 contracted missions and that Rocket Lab had sold more launches in Q1 2026 than in all of 2025 [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 Results](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/node/12416/pdf). In other words, the company's demand problem had not been a shortage of commercial interest; it had been whether engineering execution could keep pace with the market access it had already won.

## The Financial Question

The financial record through the frozen window therefore asked a narrower question than the stock chart sometimes implied. Rocket Lab had already proved it could grow revenue at scale, move up the value chain, access capital repeatedly, and convert backlog into a real industrial business. What it had not yet proved was that those strengths could outrun the cost of building Neutron. That was why the company could report record revenue, record backlog and record liquidity, while still leaving investors fixated on a rocket that had not yet flown.

chapters.title: Post-SPAC quarters through the Neutron development trajectory
chapters.body:
## The Post-SPAC Baseline

The August 2021 SPAC close had supplied roughly $777 million of gross proceeds and gave Rocket Lab both cash and public-market currency for the expansion it had already begun to sketch out [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-completes-merger-vector-acquisition-corporation). Electron scaling and Neutron development were the obvious uses of funds, but the subtler consequence was that Rocket Lab could accelerate the build-out of Space Systems without waiting for launch economics alone to finance it.

## The Acquisition Arc and Space Systems Scaling

The sequence mattered. Sinclair closed in April 2020, ASI in October 2021, PSC in December 2021, and SolAero in January 2022; Geost followed in August 2025. Revenue then stepped from $211.0 million in 2022 to $244.6 million in 2023, $436.2 million in 2024, and $601.8 million in 2025, with Space Systems contributing the majority of the mix in each of the last three years [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-satellite-hardware-manufacturer-sinclair-interplanetary/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-acquires-space-software-company-advanced-solutions-inc/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-hardware-company-planetary-systems-corporation/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-solar-power-products-company-solaero-holdings-inc/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-geost-expanding-its-national) [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm).

## Electron: Cadence as Industrial Proof

Electron's cadence became the proof that the underlying industrial system worked. Rocket Lab ended 2025 with 21 launches for the year and 79 launches overall, then reached 88 launches by 22 May 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-successfully-launches-iqps-ends-2025-21-launches-and) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/mission-success-rocket-lab-completes-9th-electron-launch). The May 2022 helicopter catch, later ocean-recovery work, and reused-engine testing showed that reusability had become a serious engineering programme even if it was not yet a routine commercial practice [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-completes-historic-mid-air-helicopter-capture-of-electron-rocket-returning-from-space/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-successfully-completes-first-test-fire-of-reused-rutherford-engine/).

## Neutron: Development and Slippage

Neutron remained the hinge. Rocket Lab kept the published payload at 13,000 kilograms to LEO, opened Launch Complex 3 in August 2025, qualified the captive fairing in December 2025, then disclosed a stage-one tank rupture during hydrostatic testing in January 2026. The company moved first launch to Q4 2026 in the February 2026 full-year results release [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/neutron/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-3-critical-milestone-path) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/node/11706/pdf) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-neutron-test-update/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial).

As of the snapshot date, Neutron had not launched. That left Rocket Lab with a real operating business, an expanding national-security franchise, and a medium-lift programme that still defined the outer boundary of the equity story.

chapters.title: Peter Beck, Adam Spice CFO, segment leadership, and the post-SPAC board
chapters.body:
## Founder Control, But With a Larger Corporate Machine Around It

Rocket Lab's leadership structure still revolved around Peter Beck. Rocket Lab's own team page described him, at the snapshot date, as Founder, President and Chief Executive Officer, and Chair of the Board. The same page said he had served on Rocket Lab's board and as President and CEO since July 2013, and had been appointed Chair in May 2021 [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about/team/). That concentration of authority was not an incidental governance quirk. It was central to how Rocket Lab had been run from private-company launch startup to public-company space contractor.

Beck's background remained as unconventional as the company he built. Rocket Lab's published biography said he began his career in 1993 as an apprentice precision engineer at Fisher & Paykel, later moved into design work, and then worked at a government research institute from 2003 on advanced composite structures and materials. The company also later made part of his founding mythology explicit in its own brand history, saying he had travelled through the United States in 2006 looking for a company that shared his view of dedicated small launch, found none, and started Rocket Lab on his return [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about/team/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/introducing-our-new-look/).

That mythmaking mattered because Beck never presented Rocket Lab as a conventional contractor that happened to find a market niche. He presented it as a company built around a contrarian first principle: that small spacecraft operators would eventually pay for control, schedule and integration rather than accept the leftovers of heavy-launch economics. Rocket Lab's own brand history kept returning to that theme, which meant the founder narrative was not merely decorative. It was the internal explanation for why the company kept reinvesting into launch infrastructure, components, spacecraft and now Neutron rather than staying a narrower launcher [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/introducing-our-new-look/).

## Chairman and CEO

The dual-role structure had always invited the standard public-market objections about board independence, but Rocket Lab had paired it with a Lead Independent Director role and a board that, by 2026, had become more aerospace- and defence-weighted than venture-weighted. Merline Saintil remained Lead Independent Director. The board roster on Rocket Lab's own corporate pages listed Nina Armagno, Edward Frank, Jon Olson, Kenneth Possenriede, Merline Saintil and Alex Slusky alongside Beck [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about/team/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/corporate-governance/board-directors).

The New Zealand state had formalised Beck's standing in June 2024, when the King's Birthday Honours list named him a Knight Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit for services to the aerospace industry, business and education [DPMC](https://www.dpmc.govt.nz/publications/kings-birthday-honours-list-2024). By the end of 2025 Rocket Lab itself had become much larger than the "small launch" label implied: the 2025 Form 10-K said the company had over 2,600 full-time permanent employees worldwide as of 31 December 2025 [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm).

That employee count mattered because it marked the scale of the organisation Beck was controlling. Rocket Lab was no longer a founder-led engineering workshop with one rocket in qualification. It was a public company operating launch sites on two continents, building spacecraft and components across the United States and New Zealand, integrating acquisitions, and carrying a nine-figure national-security backlog while developing Neutron.

It also marked the degree to which decision-making complexity had changed. By the snapshot date, Rocket Lab's leadership had to allocate capital across launch cadence, Neutron development, spacecraft production, payload manufacturing, solar expansion and government-programme execution simultaneously. Beck still dominated the strategy, but he was doing so inside a much denser operating system than the market shorthand of "founder-led rocket company" captured.

## Adam Spice and the Financial Counterweight

Adam Spice remained the indispensable financial counterpart to Beck. Rocket Lab's executive team page listed him as Chief Financial Officer, and the company had kept him in that role from before the SPAC listing through the liquidity rebuild of 2025 and 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about/team/). That continuity mattered because Rocket Lab's capital structure changed repeatedly across the public-company period: the SPAC proceeds in 2021, the 4.25% convert in 2024, the 2025 ATM programme, and the second ATM plus forward-sale transactions in 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-completes-merger-vector-acquisition-corporation) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-closing-upsized-offering-355-million) [Rocket Lab Prospectus Supplement](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/static-files/d367305d-382d-42c3-b269-969947c5f64f) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-completes-market-offering).

The financial communication style across those years was also consistent. Beck generally framed the engineering and market logic; Spice framed the liquidity, revenue mix, margin progression and forward funding. That split did not make Rocket Lab conservative. It did make the company's case to public markets more coherent than many of its space peers.

That continuity mattered because Rocket Lab's economics had become harder to explain in a single sentence. The company was simultaneously scaling a launch business, absorbing acquisition integration, taking on large fixed-price spacecraft work and funding a pre-revenue medium-lift rocket. Spice's role was not just to keep the balance sheet funded. It was to translate a mixed industrial model into numbers public investors could still underwrite quarter by quarter.

## Operational Leadership

Operationally, Frank Klein sat immediately beneath Beck in the published hierarchy as Chief Operations Officer [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about/team/). The title was broad, but the actual remit was broader still: Electron production and launch cadence, Neutron development, launch-site readiness, and the integration of Space Systems manufacturing capacity acquired and built over several years.

The corrected title line for Brian Rogers also mattered. Rocket Lab's own team page listed him as Vice President - Global Launch Services, not as Chief Revenue Officer. That distinction was not cosmetic. By May 2026 Rocket Lab had a much larger commercial and government sales apparatus across launch, spacecraft, payloads and components than a single launch-revenue title implied [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about/team/). On the launch side, Rogers' domain included multi-launch commercial agreements, the responsive-space portfolio, and the transition path from Electron to Neutron. On the strategic side, Rocket Lab had been on-ramped to NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1 on 27 March 2025, which widened the set of launch opportunities Neutron could pursue once operational [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-labs-neutron-rocket-ramped-us-space-forces-56b-national) [Space Systems Command](https://www.ssc.spaceforce.mil/Newsroom/Article/4137680/space-systems-command-on-ramps-two-new-providers-to-national-security-space-lau/).

The rest of the published executive bench underscored how much broader the company had become. Shaun D'Mello was listed as Vice President - Neutron; Brad Clevenger as Vice President - Space Systems; Cameron McCarter as Vice President - Global Supply Chain; Brian Rogers on launch; Andrew Bunker on government operations and business strategy; and several engineering, legal and operational executives supporting them [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about/team/). That was the management shape of a company trying to industrialise multiple businesses at once.

The operational read-through was that Rocket Lab no longer had the luxury of solving one problem at a time. Launch cadence, spacecraft prime work, component fulfilment, M&A integration and Neutron qualification all had to progress in parallel. The executive bench therefore mattered less as a list of titles than as evidence that Rocket Lab understood the company had become a concurrency problem as much as an engineering one.

## Board Evolution

The board also changed meaningfully through the public-company period. The current roster retained some continuity from the SPAC era through Beck, Saintil and Slusky, but Rocket Lab had added more institutional aerospace and defence experience around them. Nina Armagno joined the board in November 2023 after a senior career in the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force. Kenneth Possenriede joined in August 2024 after a long Lockheed Martin finance career. Edward Frank brought technology and R&D oversight rather than space pedigree, while Jon Olson contributed long-cycle public-company audit and finance experience [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about/team/).

The official record also showed the venture-board rotation receding. Rocket Lab disclosed in 2024 that Sven Strohband would not stand for re-election at the annual meeting, and the 2026 proxy said Matt Ocko's resignation from the board had become effective on 30 November 2025 [Rocket Lab](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000095017024045569/rklb-ex99_1.htm) [Rocket Lab 2026 Proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000162828026021744/rklb-20260327.htm). The company was not yet a classic aerospace prime, but its governance had plainly moved away from the venture-backed startup template.

That evolution was easy to underestimate because Beck still towered over the public narrative. Yet the board mix told a different story about what Rocket Lab thought it needed next: more programme oversight, more defence credibility, and more capital-markets discipline. Those are the governance tools of a company preparing for larger contracts and larger execution risk, not a company content to remain a niche launch vendor.

## The Governance Read-Through

What that left by May 2026 was a public company whose founder still dominated the operating agenda, but which no longer looked casually organised around him. The board had more range credibility, more large-programme finance experience, and more public-company infrastructure than the SPAC-era version. The executive bench had deepened around launch, spacecraft, supply chain and Neutron. The governance question therefore was no longer whether Rocket Lab had the apparatus of a public company. It did. The question was whether that apparatus was strong enough to support Beck's next act: turning Neutron from a capital programme into an operating business.

chapters.title: NASA, US Space Force, commercial satellite operators, and the propellant-and-components supply
chapters.body:
Rocket Lab's customer list, read through the filings and official releases rather than through ticker-message-board mythology, showed a company that had crossed into three adjacent roles at once: launch provider, spacecraft prime, and supplier of critical components into other primes' programmes. That transition had been deliberate. Beck had argued for years that launch alone was too narrow and too cyclical a base. By the frozen snapshot date, the contract record showed the thesis being implemented in full.

## NASA: CAPSTONE, ESCAPADE, and the Civil-Space Proof Points

NASA remained one of the clearest validation customers. In February 2020 the agency awarded Rocket Lab a $9.95 million contract to launch CAPSTONE from Virginia, a small lunar mission that would use Electron and Photon to send a CubeSat toward near-rectilinear halo orbit around the Moon [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-contract-to-launch-cubesat-to-moon-from-virginia/). CAPSTONE launched in June 2022 and, more importantly for Rocket Lab, validated Photon as a serious beyond-LEO platform rather than just an upper-stage derivative.

The relationship deepened. Rocket Lab later said the ESCAPADE twin spacecraft it built for the University of California Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory had been successfully launched toward Mars in late 2025 and were fully commissioned at Earth-Sun L2 by February 2026 before handover for science operations [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-completes-spacecraft-commissioning-for-nasas-escapade-mars-mission/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial). NASA also remained a recurring launch customer through other missions, including Aspera and LOXSAT in Rocket Lab's forward mission materials by the snapshot date [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/missions/launches/).

## SolAero, Albuquerque, and the Semiconductor Supply Chain

The deeper civil-space relationship ran through solar supply rather than launch. When Rocket Lab closed SolAero in January 2022, it took ownership of a strategically scarce U.S. producer of space-grade solar cells and panels [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-solar-power-products-company-solaero-holdings-inc/). NIST later said the Albuquerque facility was selected for up to $23.9 million of CHIPS funding to modernise and expand space-grade semiconductor production. NIST also described the investment as supporting the domestic supply of radiation-resistant compound semiconductors used in spacecraft power systems [NIST](https://www.nist.gov/chips/rocket-lab-new-mexico-albuquerque).

That made SolAero more than a component acquisition. It made Rocket Lab one of a very small number of U.S. producers with direct leverage over a supply chain the government increasingly treated as strategic. By August 2025 Rocket Lab itself was explicitly tying the Albuquerque expansion to national-security demand for solar cells and to the Geost payload business [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-expanded-us-investments-national-security).

## SDA and the National-Security Prime Franchise

The most important change in Rocket Lab's customer mix came from the U.S. national-security establishment. In January 2024 the Space Development Agency awarded Rocket Lab National Security a fixed-price OTA worth approximately $515 million to build and operate 18 Tranche 2 Transport Layer-Beta satellites, with launches due no later than July 2027 [SDA](https://www.sda.mil/space-development-agency-makes-third-award-to-build-18-additional-beta-variant-satellites-for-tranche-2-transport-layer/). That was Rocket Lab's first major disclosed programme as a spacecraft prime rather than a subsystem provider.

Then in December 2025 the company won an $816 million SDA award to build 18 Tracking Layer Tranche 3 satellites for missile warning and tracking. Rocket Lab described it as its largest contract to date and said the work could pull additional merchant-supply opportunities from the rest of its portfolio as other primes on the tranche sourced solar solutions, software and attitude-control hardware [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-awarded-816m-prime-contract-build-missile-defense) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/missions/launches/sda-tracking-layer-tranche-3/).

These were not symbolic awards. They were large enough to change the revenue mix and to demonstrate that Rocket Lab could sit across the table from customers that historically defaulted to Lockheed, Northrop, Boeing or L3Harris. By Q1 2026 the company said backlog had climbed to $2.22 billion, with Space Systems still the larger component [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm).

## VICTUS HAZE and HASTE

Launch work for defence customers had become more consequential too. In April 2024 Rocket Lab disclosed a $32 million Space Systems Command contract for VICTUS HAZE, an end-to-end tactically responsive space mission that required Rocket Lab to design, build, launch and operate a rendezvous-and-proximity-operations-capable spacecraft on Electron within 24 hours of a go order [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-selected-space-systems-command-build-and-launch). That contract mattered because it combined spacecraft, launch and operations in one award - a direct test of the integrated model.

In March 2026 Rocket Lab added another defence milestone: a four-year, $190 million contract for 20 HASTE launches under MACH-TB 2.0. The company said the award took its launch manifest to more than 70 missions in backlog [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-secures-190m-contract-20x-haste-launches-cements). HASTE had effectively become a separate business line: less visible than Electron in public imagination, but strategically important because it placed Rocket Lab in the middle of one of Washington's highest-priority test infrastructure problems.

## Commercial Constellation Customers

Commercially, the pattern that mattered most was repetition. Synspective expanded its contract in September 2025, taking total booked Electron launches to 21 through the end of the decade [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-and-synspective-strike-another-10-launch-deal). iQPS continued to add missions, and by August 2025 Rocket Lab said it had already flown the fifth dedicated iQPS mission and the fourth for that customer during 2025 alone [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/mission-success-rocket-labs-latest-constellation-deployment). Capella had signed a dedicated four-launch agreement in early 2023 [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-signs-multi-launch-deal-to-deploy-satellite-constellation-for-capella-space/). BlackSky added another four dedicated Electron launches in February 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-secures-latest-multi-launch-contract-blacksky-4x).

What these customers were buying was not simply lift capacity. They were buying schedule certainty, orbit specificity, and a service architecture that increasingly let Rocket Lab bundle launch with separation systems, spacecraft components, and in some cases complete spacecraft. That was why commercial relationships persisted even as Falcon 9 offered lower cost per kilogram.

## Globalstar and the Spacecraft-Prime Test

One of the clearest examples of Rocket Lab's move up the stack came from the Globalstar replenishment programme. Rocket Lab said in its first-quarter 2022 results that it had been awarded a $143 million subcontract by MDA to design and build 17 spacecraft buses for the Globalstar constellation [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-first-quarter-2022-financial-results-and). The second-quarter 2022 release clarified that these were 17 spacecraft buses for approximately 500-kilogram satellites and that the production work was part of the new Long Beach constellation facility ramp [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-second-quarter-2022-financial-results-and).

The programme later became a real execution test. Globalstar's 2025 Form 10-K said the company was contractually entitled to receive liquidated damages from MDA Space because delivery milestones had been missed under the satellite procurement agreement and that, by year-end 2025, accepted milestones totalled $258.3 million [Globalstar 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1366868/000136686826000012/gsat-20251231.htm). Rocket Lab was not the prime contractor to Globalstar, but it was the disclosed spacecraft-bus supplier on the programme. That made the delay language relevant to any assessment of Rocket Lab's ability to execute at higher spacecraft volumes.

## Propellant and Industrial Inputs

The physical supply chain also deserved more precision. Electron used LOX and kerosene, exactly as Rocket Lab's product page said, on an 18 metre vehicle with 13,000 kilograms of wet mass [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/electron/). Neutron switched to methane and LOX. Launch Complex 3 in Virginia was described by Rocket Lab as a launch, test and landing facility purpose-built for that larger reusable vehicle [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-3-critical-milestone-path) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/neutron/).

On the manufacturing side, Rocket Lab's 144,000-plus square foot Engine Development Center in Long Beach opened in October 2023 after the company took over the former Virgin Orbit facility and bought assets and equipment for $16.1 million. Rocket Lab said the site would support high-rate Rutherford production and development and production of Archimedes [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-opens-engine-development-center-in-long-beach/). New Zealand retained a parallel role in launch operations, composites and production support, which meant Rocket Lab's industrial map remained trans-Pacific even as national-security customers pulled more programme gravity toward U.S. soil.

The sum of those relationships was the real supply-chain picture. Rocket Lab had become embedded with NASA, the Space Force, SDA, commercial constellation operators and other spacecraft primes not because any single product dominated, but because the company increasingly sold multiple layers of the same mission.

chapters.title: Where Rocket Lab sits against SpaceX, Firefly, Astra, and the broader launch landscape
chapters.body:
## The Field Narrowed Faster Than the Pitch Decks Expected

When Electron first reached orbit in January 2018, the Western small-launch market looked crowded with aspirants. By the frozen snapshot date in May 2026, operational reality had thinned that list sharply. Rocket Lab had survived the attrition and had done so with a flight record that no other dedicated Western small-launch company had matched.

The important distinction was not merely that weaker competitors had failed. It was that Rocket Lab had turned cadence into a barrier. The company ended 2025 having flown 21 missions across Electron and HASTE with 100% mission success for the year, reached its 80th Electron launch in January 2026, its 84th in March, and its 88th by 22 May 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-successfully-launches-iqps-ends-2025-21-launches-and) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-delivers-mission-success-first-launch-2026-new) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/mission-success-rocket-lab-launches-latest-satellite-0) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/mission-success-rocket-lab-completes-9th-electron-launch).

## Small Launch: Electron's Moat

Electron's moat was not payload mass. Rocket Lab's own published figure remained 300 kilograms to LEO, smaller than Firefly Alpha and far smaller than Falcon 9 [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/electron/). The moat was operational maturity: two launch sites, repeat commercial customers, repeat defence customers, and a service designed around dedicated scheduling rather than shared manifest economics. By 2026, customers such as Synspective, iQPS, Capella, BlackSky and HawkEye 360 were booking multiple dedicated launches rather than opportunistic one-offs [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-and-synspective-strike-another-10-launch-deal) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/iqps-books-three-new-launches-electron-extending-multi-year) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-signs-multi-launch-deal-to-deploy-satellite-constellation-for-capella-space/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-secures-latest-multi-launch-contract-blacksky-4x).

Firefly was still the most credible small-launch peer in the United States, with a larger published payload and a meaningful tactically responsive launch demonstration on Victus Nox. But Firefly had not yet shown Electron's flight-rate consistency or accumulated customer repetition. Rocket Lab's ability to keep launching from both Mahia and Wallops, and to move from commercial to NASA to national-security payloads without changing industrial base, was the more durable competitive asset.

That was why comparing launch vehicles on payload alone missed the commercial point. Many customers were not shopping for the cheapest kilogram. They were shopping for a launch date, an orbit, a licensing path and a counterpart that could actually deliver without waiting for a rideshare stack to fill. Rocket Lab's advantage in small launch came from compressing those uncertainties, even if a heavy launcher looked superior on headline transport economics.

## Medium Launch: The Falcon 9 Problem Still Existed

Neutron's competitive logic was clear even before first flight. Rocket Lab wanted a reusable medium-launch vehicle that could compete where Electron could not: constellation replenishment, higher-value government payloads, and missions that were too large for small launch but did not require heavy lift. The company's own published payload number for Neutron remained 13,000 kilograms to LEO in reusable configuration [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/neutron/).

But the competitive problem did not soften just because the product thesis made sense. Falcon 9 remained the market benchmark on both cadence and cost. ULA's Vulcan, Arianespace's Ariane 6, and Blue Origin's New Glenn all operated in adjacent weight classes, yet none had matched SpaceX's combination of rhythm, cost absorption and launch heritage by the snapshot date. That left Neutron with a specific opening rather than a broad one: customers who wanted another Western medium-lift option, and government buyers who wanted supplier diversity, but who still needed a real vehicle on the pad before contracts could convert into routine missions.

Rocket Lab had done the commercial pre-work. Neutron was on-ramped to NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1 in March 2025. The company had already booked dedicated Neutron launch service agreements, including a multi-launch constellation deal disclosed in 2024 and further Neutron launch sales disclosed in Q1 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-labs-neutron-rocket-ramped-us-space-forces-56b-national) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 Results](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/node/12416/pdf). What it had not yet done, by definition, was fly.

The market was therefore being asked to separate two different questions. One was whether Neutron's commercial thesis made sense. By the snapshot date, the answer to that was largely yes: the Space Force had on-ramped it, customers had signed for it, and Rocket Lab had built real infrastructure around it. The second question was whether the engineering schedule would hold tightly enough for those theoretical wins to turn into a durable operating franchise. That answer remained unproven until flight.

## Space Systems: Competing Up the Stack

Rocket Lab's Space Systems business competed in a different arena altogether. There the reference set was not Astra or Firefly, but a mix of defence primes, specialist subsystem vendors, and satellite builders. The company's edge came from vertical integration and from its willingness to serve as both merchant supplier and system integrator.
