Reaction wheels, star trackers, software, separation systems, solar products, spacecraft buses, payloads and launch could now be sold in combinations that few comparably sized public companies could match [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about-us/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/about/team/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-geost-expanding-its-national).

The two largest public markers of that shift were the $515 million SDA Transport Layer award in January 2024 and the $816 million Tracking Layer award in December 2025 [SDA](https://www.sda.mil/space-development-agency-makes-third-award-to-build-18-additional-beta-variant-satellites-for-tranche-2-transport-layer/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-awarded-816m-prime-contract-build-missile-defense). Those contracts did not make Rocket Lab a legacy prime. They did show that it had become something more dangerous to incumbents than a launch boutique: a fast-moving integrated competitor with growing government trust.

That gave Rocket Lab a competitive position at multiple price points. At the low end it could sell components into someone else's platform. In the middle it could sell a spacecraft bus or an integrated mission architecture. At the top it could now chase prime contracts that bundled buses, payloads, launch and operations. Few companies of comparable size had that ladder, which was why Rocket Lab's competitive set looked different depending on which layer of the stack a customer wanted to buy.

## The Competitive Read-Through

Rocket Lab's competitive position by May 2026 therefore rested on three facts. First, Electron had become the operational standard-bearer in Western dedicated small launch. Second, Space Systems had grown into the larger business and the broader strategic wedge. Third, Neutron remained the unresolved multiplier. If it flew close to the revised Q4 2026 target and proved out reusability over time, Rocket Lab's addressable market would widen substantially. If it slipped again, the company would still own a credible small-launch and space-systems franchise - just not the full medium-lift challenge to SpaceX that the equity story increasingly presumed.

That was the crucial boundary. Rocket Lab had already won the right to be discussed as a serious space-industrial company. The part still priced on faith was the leap from that position into a repeatable medium-lift competitor.

chapters.title: From 2018 Electron through 2021 SPAC, acquisitions, and Neutron development
chapters.body:
## Electron Found Product-Market Fit Before the Market Said It Had

The first durable catalyst in Rocket Lab's story had not been the public listing. It had been operational proof. "Still Testing" reached orbit on 21 January 2018, "It's Business Time" followed in November 2018, and by the end of 2025 Electron and HASTE had delivered 21 launches for the year with 100% mission success [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/missions/launches/still-testing/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/missions/launches/its-business-time/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-successfully-launches-iqps-ends-2025-21-launches-and). That cadence, more than any slide deck, was what made the public-market listing plausible.

## The SPAC and the Space Systems Build-Out

The August 2021 merger with Vector Acquisition Corporation then supplied the balance-sheet flexibility to widen the company beyond launch, delivering approximately $777 million of gross proceeds [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-completes-merger-vector-acquisition-corporation). The acquisition arc that followed was more precise than earlier drafts suggested: Sinclair in April 2020, ASI in October 2021, PSC in December 2021, SolAero in January 2022, and Geost in August 2025 [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-satellite-hardware-manufacturer-sinclair-interplanetary/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-acquires-space-software-company-advanced-solutions-inc/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-hardware-company-planetary-systems-corporation/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-solar-power-products-company-solaero-holdings-inc/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-geost-expanding-its-national). By 2025, Space Systems had become the larger revenue segment.

## Neutron Stayed the Highest-Impact Catalyst

Neutron remained the biggest single forward catalyst because it was the only disclosed programme capable of changing Rocket Lab's launch class. The company opened Launch Complex 3 in August 2025, qualified the attached fairing in December 2025, then disclosed a stage-one tank rupture during qualification testing in January 2026. In February 2026 it shifted first launch to Q4 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-3-critical-milestone-path) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/node/11706/pdf) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-neutron-test-update/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial).

## What Investors Actually Needed to Watch

Three catalysts therefore mattered most by the snapshot date: Neutron's path from qualification to first flight; continued conversion of national-security demand into backlog, especially across SDA, VICTUS HAZE and HASTE; and proof that Space Systems could keep expanding faster than launch without sacrificing execution [SDA](https://www.sda.mil/space-development-agency-makes-third-award-to-build-18-additional-beta-variant-satellites-for-tranche-2-transport-layer/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-selected-space-systems-command-build-and-launch) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-secures-190m-contract-20x-haste-launches-cements). Everything else, including the stock's volatility, was secondary to those operating questions.

chapters.title: Electron, Neutron, Photon, and the Space Systems components IP
chapters.body:
## Rutherford and the Electron Stack

Rocket Lab's first durable piece of proprietary technical identity remained Rutherford. The company described Electron at the snapshot date as the world's first orbital rocket powered by 3D-printed, electric-pump-fed engines and continued to publish the Rutherford cycle as a core differentiator [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/electron/). Earlier Rocket Lab technical material put the sea-level Rutherford at roughly 24 to 25 kilonewtons of thrust, the vacuum version at 343 seconds of specific impulse, and the dry engine mass at 35 kilograms. The 2019 100th-engine milestone release also reiterated that the company's primary Rutherford components were produced through additive manufacturing and that major components could be printed in roughly 24 hours [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-celebrates-100th-rutherford-engine-build/).

The more important point was not novelty for its own sake. Electric pumping let Rocket Lab simplify a small orbital engine enough to manufacture it at higher rates and lower unit complexity than a comparable turbomachinery-heavy design. Coupled with Electron's carbon-composite tanks and structures, that gave the company a technical package that was unusually suited to repeatable small-launch production [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/electron/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-celebrates-100th-rutherford-engine-build/).

That design philosophy also explained why Rocket Lab kept talking about vertical integration as a technical tool rather than just a margin lever. The company was not merely buying suppliers to capture economics. It was trying to control enough of propulsion, structures, software and spacecraft hardware to iterate faster across the whole mission stack. Rutherford was the earliest visible example of that approach, but by 2026 it had become the template for much of the wider business.

## Recovery Work as Technology Development

Rocket Lab had also used Electron as a reusability laboratory. It completed the first mid-air helicopter capture of a returning orbital-class booster in May 2022, later continued with ocean recoveries, and in 2022 successfully test-fired a reused Rutherford engine. In 2024 it said a previously flown Electron tank had been returned to the standard production line in preparation for the first reflight of a recovered stage [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-completes-historic-mid-air-helicopter-capture-of-electron-rocket-returning-from-space/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-successfully-completes-first-test-fire-of-reused-rutherford-engine/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-returns-previously-flown-electron-to-production-line-in-preparation-for-first-reflight/). That work had not yet turned into routine commercial booster reuse, but it had created a data set that informed Neutron's much more ambitious recovery architecture.

## Archimedes and Neutron

Neutron was where Rocket Lab's research and development burden became strategically visible. The company's published Neutron page described a reusable, methane-fuelled rocket capable of carrying 13,000 kilograms to LEO [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/launch/neutron/). Rocket Lab completed the first successful hot fire of Archimedes in August 2024 and later kept accumulating qualification milestones across structures, launch infrastructure and fairing hardware [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-completes-successful-first-hot-fire-archimedes-engine) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-3-critical-milestone-path).

The standout structural idea was the attached fairing. Rocket Lab's December 2025 qualification release said the "Hungry Hippo" captive fairing remained attached to Neutron's first stage throughout launch and landing, opening to release the upper stage and payload and then closing again before return to Earth as part of a single reusable vehicle [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/node/11706/pdf). That was not simply a branding flourish. It was central to Rocket Lab's claim that Neutron could cut turnaround complexity relative to vehicles that jettisoned and later recovered separate fairing halves.

The development programme still encountered a major setback. On 21 January 2026 Rocket Lab disclosed that the stage-one tank had ruptured during hydrostatic qualification testing. The company said there was no major facility damage and that the next tank was already in production, but the February 2026 full-year results release later moved the first-launch target to Q4 2026 [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-neutron-test-update/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial).

That incident clarified where the hardest technical risk still sat. Archimedes had already hot-fired, and Launch Complex 3 physically existed. The rupture showed that large reusable structures, qualification margins and full-vehicle industrialisation still held the power to move the schedule. In other words, Rocket Lab's remaining problem was not whether it could design interesting space hardware. It was whether it could close the last gap between ambitious design and routine heavy-duty manufacturing.

## Photon, Curie and Deep-Space Ambition

Rocket Lab's spacecraft intellectual property sat beside launch rather than beneath it. Photon evolved from Electron's Kick Stage into a standalone bus with power, propulsion, communications and mission-management capability. CAPSTONE validated the architecture on a lunar mission in 2022, and ESCAPADE's twin Rocket Lab-built spacecraft were fully commissioned at Earth-Sun L2 by February 2026 [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-contract-to-launch-cubesat-to-moon-from-virginia/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-completes-spacecraft-commissioning-for-nasas-escapade-mars-mission/). The point was not just that Rocket Lab could launch its own spacecraft. It was that it had learned to sell mission architecture, bus integration and operations as part of the same industrial system.

## Components: Where Vertical Integration Became Real

The components stack had become broad enough to constitute a separate technology franchise. Sinclair added star trackers and reaction wheels. PSC added flight-proven separation systems. SolAero brought radiation-resistant solar cells, panels and composite structures. ASI supplied flight software, simulation and GNC tools. Geost added electro-optical and infrared payload expertise. In April 2026 Rocket Lab introduced Gauss, an internally engineered Hall-effect propulsion system, which was important partly because it showed the company closing a propulsion gap through in-house development rather than through another acquisition [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-satellite-hardware-manufacturer-sinclair-interplanetary/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-hardware-company-planetary-systems-corporation/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-of-space-solar-power-products-company-solaero-holdings-inc/) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-acquires-space-software-company-advanced-solutions-inc/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-closes-acquisition-geost-expanding-its-national) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-unveils-new-electric-propulsion-satellite-thruster).

Rocket Lab's own spacecraft materials showed how these components fed into reusable platform families. Explorer underpinned CAPSTONE and ESCAPADE. Lightning was described as the basis for Globalstar and the tailored SDA Transport Layer platform. Pioneer supported Varda's re-entry missions. Photon remained the core integrated launch-plus-spacecraft solution. The same page said Rocket Lab had more than 40 spacecraft in backlog and 1,700 spacecraft globally featuring Rocket Lab components [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/spacecraft). That was strong evidence that the company's R&D base was creating both merchant component demand and platform-level reuse.

## R&D Against Revenue

The expense lines showed how hard Rocket Lab was still pushing. R&D expense, net, rose from $119.1 million in 2023 to $174.4 million in 2024 and $270.7 million in 2025, then to $80.5 million in Q1 2026 alone [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm). The filings tied the 2026 increase principally to Neutron development progress, staff growth, and prototype work on spacecraft and component products. That meant Rocket Lab was funding two forms of innovation simultaneously: a medium-lift launch vehicle that had not yet flown, and a space-systems portfolio that was already generating most of the company's revenue.

| Period | R&D Expense | Revenue | R&D / Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $119.1M | $244.6M | 48.7% |
| FY2024 | $174.4M | $436.2M | 40.0% |
| FY2025 | $270.7M | $601.8M | 45.0% |
| Q1 2026 | $80.5M | $200.3M | 40.2% |

The resulting intellectual-property picture was therefore less about patents in isolation and more about stack ownership. By the snapshot date, Rocket Lab owned meaningful pieces of propulsion, structures, launch operations, spacecraft buses, solar power, separation systems, software, guidance and payloads. That breadth was expensive. It was also the technical foundation for the company's claim that it had become an end-to-end space company rather than a small rocket with ambitions.

The technical and financial stories were inseparable. Rocket Lab's R&D line looked heavy precisely because the company was trying to own more of the stack at once. The question for investors was not whether the company was spending to innovate. It plainly was. The question was whether enough of that innovation would mature into products with repeat economics before Neutron consumed too much of the upside.

chapters.title: Neutron development risk, SpaceX competition, capex intensity, customer concentration
chapters.body:
## Neutron Remained the First Risk

The central risk was still Neutron. Rocket Lab had opened Launch Complex 3, qualified the captive fairing, and on-ramped the vehicle to NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1 before first flight, but the January 2026 stage-one tank rupture showed that qualification risk had not been abstract [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-3-critical-milestone-path) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/node/11706/pdf) [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-neutron-test-update/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-labs-neutron-rocket-ramped-us-space-forces-56b-national). The schedule had already moved from 2024 to the second half of 2025 and then to Q4 2026. A further slip would not destroy Rocket Lab's existing business, but it would defer the highest-value part of the thesis yet again.

## The SpaceX Problem

Even a successful first launch would not eliminate the market challenge. Falcon 9 still dominated the medium-lift market on cadence, price absorption and launch heritage. Neutron's customer pitch rested on mission dedication, government demand for alternatives, and a reusable architecture that had not yet been proven in service. Until Rocket Lab demonstrated repeated Neutron operations, the unit economics remained a model rather than a track record.

## Capital Intensity and Dilution

Rocket Lab had materially reduced funding risk through the 2025 and 2026 ATM programmes, but it had done so at the cost of dilution. The company sold roughly $749.4 million of stock under the prior ATM programme during 2025 and then another roughly $474 million under the 2026 ATM before entering forward-sale arrangements tied to a further 7.45 million shares [Rocket Lab Prospectus Supplement](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/static-files/d367305d-382d-42c3-b269-969947c5f64f) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-completes-market-offering). That financing made the balance sheet stronger. It also meant that future returns depended not only on Neutron working, but on Neutron working well enough to justify a much larger equity base.

## Customer Concentration and Government Timing

Government demand was an advantage, but it also introduced concentration and timing risk. The March 2026 Form 10-Q said one government customer accounted for 36% of total revenue in the quarter, and Kratos SRE accounted for 21% of accounts receivable at quarter-end [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm). Government contracts also moved at the speed of appropriations, milestone acceptance, programme reviews and procurement politics. A company can have a record backlog and still experience working-capital volatility when the customer base leans this heavily on state buyers.

## Execution Risk in Space Systems

Space Systems had become the larger segment, which meant it had also become a larger risk surface. The Globalstar/MDA programme illustrated that clearly. Globalstar's 2025 10-K said it was entitled to seek liquidated damages from MDA because delivery milestones had been missed on the replenishment-satellite programme [Globalstar 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1366868/000136686826000012/gsat-20251231.htm). Rocket Lab was not the programme prime to Globalstar, but it was the disclosed spacecraft-bus supplier. That showed the kind of problem that emerges when a company moves from selling parts and launches to carrying higher responsibility in larger spacecraft builds.

## Launch Risk Never Vanished

Electron's record had become strong enough to make launch failure seem exceptional rather than probable, but it would have remained financially and reputationally damaging. By the snapshot date Rocket Lab had reached 88 launches overall [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/mission-success-rocket-lab-completes-9th-electron-launch). That history gave the company credibility. It did not repeal the physics. A launch failure, a systemic spacecraft fault, or a critical supplier interruption could still hit both margins and backlog conversion.

chapters.title: Neutron first launch, Space Systems scaling, and the 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Business Entered 2026 With More Than One Engine

The reason Rocket Lab still attracted medium-term strategic interest after repeated Neutron slips was that the company entered 2026 with more than one operating engine. Electron was a real launch franchise. Space Systems was already the larger revenue segment. National-security customers had started to use Rocket Lab as a prime contractor rather than merely as a specialist launch vendor [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [SDA](https://www.sda.mil/space-development-agency-makes-third-award-to-build-18-additional-beta-variant-satellites-for-tranche-2-transport-layer/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-awarded-816m-prime-contract-build-missile-defense).

## Neutron Was Still the Wager

That said, Neutron remained the factor most likely to reshape the equity story. Rocket Lab's own timeline had shifted from 2024, to later 2025, to Q4 2026 after the January 2026 tank-test rupture [Rocket Lab](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-neutron-test-update/) [Rocket Lab](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial). If the vehicle reached first flight on the revised schedule and then moved toward operational cadence, Rocket Lab would gain access to a much larger slice of constellation, exploration and defence launch demand. If it slipped materially again, Rocket Lab would still own a valuable launch-plus-space-systems franchise - but one without the launch-class expansion that justified so much of the 2025-2026 capital spend.

## Space Systems Looked More Durable Than the Market Used to Assume

The less glamorous part of the outlook was arguably the sturdier one. Space Systems had grown to $402.8 million of revenue in 2025 and $136.7 million in Q1 2026, backed by contracts that ranged from Globalstar buses to SDA constellations to merchant supply of separation systems, solar products, software and payloads [Rocket Lab 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000013/rklb-20251231.htm) [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm). Even if Neutron's schedule moved again, that segment had already shown it could scale.

There were reasons to be cautious. Execution on large spacecraft programmes still had to mature. Margin expansion would have to compete with continuing R&D intensity. Government concentration meant backlog quality and revenue timing would matter as much as headline totals. But by the snapshot date Rocket Lab was no longer reliant on a single product category to justify its existence.

The balance sheet bought management time to prove that point. With roughly $1.48 billion of cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities at 31 March 2026, plus more than $2.2 billion of backlog, Rocket Lab had more room than most emerging space companies to absorb programme volatility and keep funding development [Rocket Lab Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000181999426000028/rklb-20260331.htm). That did not remove execution risk, but it did make the company less hostage to the next financing window than it had been a year earlier.

## The Core Question

The five-year question therefore had two layers. The first was whether Neutron could turn Rocket Lab into a real medium-lift competitor. The second was whether the company could keep converting its integrated stack - launch, spacecraft, payloads, components and operations - into a business whose economics improved even before Neutron reached routine service. The first question would dominate headlines. The second was what would determine whether Rocket Lab remained strategically valuable even if the first one took longer than planned.

Neutron would decide the upside ceiling. Electron, HASTE and Space Systems would decide how resilient the company looked while waiting to find out. Backlog and liquidity bought time, but they did not supply proof of execution. Customers had already validated much of the stack; the remaining unknown was whether launch-class expansion could be turned into schedule discipline.

financials.key_finding: Rocket Lab is pre-profit. Revenue has grown substantially from the post-SPAC baseline through 2023-2025, driven by Space Systems segment expansion (acquired companies plus Photon platform) plus Electron launch cadence growth. Neutron development is the principal forward strategic event — first launch slippages have been disclosed.
structural_observations: Rocket Lab is the principal listed US small-launch and broader space systems pure-play.
The Space Systems segment has scaled substantially via acquisitions (Sinclair Interplanetary, ASI, Solero, Plasma propulsion) plus organic Photon platform development.
Electron has launched over 50 missions through 2025; competitive landscape includes Firefly Aerospace, Astra (struggling), and broader.
Neutron is targeting first launch late 2025 / 2026 — slippages reported. Targeting the medium launch market dominated by SpaceX Falcon 9.
Cash position and capital structure: substantial cash from post-SPAC equity plus subsequent debt and equity raises; Neutron development capex is the principal forward use of cash.

leadership.key_finding: Rocket Lab's leadership is structured around founder CEO Peter Beck — the New Zealand engineer who founded the company in 2006 and has continued as CEO through the SPAC listing and into the post-public period. Beck also serves as Chairman of the Board — a dual-role structure that signals continuity of founder operational control through the multi-year Neutron development programme. CFO Adam Spice joined in 2018 (pre-SPAC) providing financial continuity. The executive team includes COO Frank Klein, Chief Revenue Officer Brian Rogers, and senior leadership across launch operations, space systems, and the broader operational organisation. The board includes directors with aerospace, defence, and venture capital backgrounds calibrated for the company's strategic trajectory.

leadership.board_composition_observation: Rocket Lab's board pairs founder CEO/Chairman Peter Beck with venture capital partners (Cowan Bessemer, Ocko DCVC, Strohband Khosla) representing the early-stage investor pedigree that supported the company's pre-public growth. The composition reflects the SPAC-era assembly of a board that combines founder operational control with venture capital governance perspective; subsequent board additions through the post-SPAC period have layered additional aerospace, defence, and broader operational experience. The forward governance trajectory through the Neutron commercial debut and beyond depends on continued Beck operational leadership plus the broader board composition's support of the multi-year strategic execution.
